doc.title: Oliver Nelson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 10, 2020

title: Television work, Stanley Wilson and residuals
summary: Royalties from The Six Million Dollar Man, writing on the spot for Longstreet, mentor Stanley Wilson at Universal, other composers in Los Angeles, and Ironside.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Well because they had to be prepared to do pretty much anything. It’s interesting you mention “The Six Million Dollar Man.” From a family royalty standpoint we still get paid for that stuff. Universal owns the rights to the music itself, but we get half of what they get, which is a really good thing. Mark Wahlberg was scheduled to make a Six

Billion Dollar Man and they’ve been talking about this for twenty years. But they were actually close this time. So I keep in touch with the Universal guy to see if they started and they said no they’re still in post-production. And of course then Covid came so I don’t know what’s going to happen with it. But I was telling some of my students actually yesterday, he did a show called “Longstreet” with a guy names James Franciscus. He was a blind insurance investigator and he was covering this guy that was in jail but he was a trumpet player. So they had this scene where they said, “You know what, Oliver, we really need some music for this trumpet player to be thinking about and playing in this cell.” You’ve got guys in the soundstage, everybody sitting there, he sits down and just starts — and he has to come up with something immediately for the producer to be able to make this scene work. So he really honed his craft with that stuff. When he first went to Hollywood, Monk, it’s really interesting, he said he had no clue. Everything, you know you’ve got to soft whisper a love song and everything’s loud. So he had to learn. He had a couple of mentors but one in particular, a guy named Stanley Wilson, he was the head of Universal Television. And Stanley kind of put his arm around my Dad and Stanley kind of took him under his wings and he kind of went from show to show to show. Because Quincy had already been out there. Benny Carter was out there. J.J. moved out there. Benny Golson moved out there, Tom MacIntosh was out there. And a lot of those guys weren’t even playing instruments anymore. You know they were composers. So Benny kind of gave everybody the start because he was one of the first African Americans to go out there and compose. And then Quincy followed him. And Quincy got some really great breaks with “The Pawnbroker” and a lot of the movies that he got a chance to do. But Dad wrote the inside music for “Ironside.” Because Quincy wrote the theme song for that. He wrote I’ll bet you for seven, eight years. I mean it was a long — it might not have been that long but it was a pretty long time. And that’s the beauty of residuals. I tell my students that our portfolio now as the music coming [inaudible] has got two components. It’s got the jazz component, then it’s got the television component. We don’t control a lot of the television component, but the television component by far brings in more royalty money than the jazz component any day of the week and on Sunday.
